messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ingrid is a 54-year-old married European-American woman who has worked as a head chef at a mid-sized restaurant for nearly two decades. She presented for intake following a referral from her primary care physician, reporting severe and persistent psychological distress following an assault committed by a male colleague she had known and trusted for several years. Her PCL-5 score of 68 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerges across the first sessions is one of a woman whose interior world has been comprehensively reorganised around a single act of violence.

The assault occurred approximately fourteen months ago, after a late closing shift. The kitchen had emptied, and Ingrid was alone with the colleague finishing inventory — a routine she had repeated dozens of times without incident. What happened that night resists her own narration. She cannot sequence it, cannot find words that hold it still. What she retains instead are fragments: the sound of the walk-in refrigerator door, a particular angle of fluorescent light, the cold of the stainless steel counter pressing against her back, and a bodily knowledge so complete that when any of these fragments surface, she feels her body curl and brace as though the event is still happening. The memory does not come as story. It comes as posture.

In the months that followed, Ingrid found that the assault had not simply left a wound — it had rewritten the terms by which she understood other people. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like hard-won wisdom, that trust is a vulnerability that gets exploited. She had trusted this man. She had worked beside him for years, shared meals with him, advocated for his promotion. The betrayal was not incidental to her suffering; it was its centre. From this conviction — that people cannot be trusted, that harm can come from anyone, that she had been naive to believe otherwise — her perception of threat had expanded outward. Strangers approaching the pass-through window at the restaurant now activated a vigilance she could not override. Any unexpected movement nearby — a line cook turning suddenly, a server reaching past her — produced a full-body startle response that left her shaking and embarrassed. She was superalert at all times, scanning exits, tracking the position of every man in the room.

This state of chronic watchfulness fed directly back into her memory. When Ingrid was on high alert — which was most of her working day — the fragments came more readily, more insistently, and with them the physical reenactment: the bracing, the constriction in her chest, the sense of weight. The hypervigilance that was meant to protect her instead kept returning her to the very experience she was trying to outrun. And each time the memory surfaced in that embodied, wordless way, her conviction deepened — people cannot be trusted, she is not safe, the world confirmed this — which in turn sharpened her threat perception further, tightening the whole arrangement.

She began avoiding situations at work that she could not fully control. She stopped taking closing shifts. She refused to be in the walk-in refrigerator with any male colleague present, a change that her sous-chef noticed and that has generated friction on the team. Certain conversation topics — anything touching on workplace relationships, on loyalty, on what happened that night — caused her to go silent or leave the room. When her husband tried to draw her out emotionally, to get close in the way they once had, she found herself pulling back sharply; emotional intimacy had become a trigger in its own right, a reminder of the openness she had shown the man who harmed her. These appraisals of danger and betrayal were not only conclusions she had reached — they were lenses that actively shaped which situations felt unbearable, which conversations felt like threats, which moments of closeness felt like exposure.

What finally brought Ingrid to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she snapped at a young male apprentice who had touched her shoulder to get her attention. She saw his face — startled, confused, a little hurt — and recognised something she did not want to become. She is most afraid that she is permanently changed. She hopes, tentatively, to find a way back to the kitchen she once loved.
